CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the G20 Osaka meeting (June 28-29) with a firm but constructive negotiating posture. Signal willingness to increase US commodity purchases and discuss some IP/tech-transfer concerns, but insist on Huawei delisting and no $300B tariffs as prerequisites for any deal. Do not announce retaliatory measures before the meeting — preserve the unreliable entity list and rare earth threats as unplayed leverage cards. The goal is to secure a truce that freezes escalation and restarts substantive talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China's interests is HIGH (+0.55) but not yet existential, for two reasons.

First, the Huawei Entity List action (May 16) is the most damaging single escalation — it targets China's national tech champion and directly threatens Made in China 2025 ambitions. Evidence shows Huawei has already cut supply chain orders by ~30%, suspended some smartphone production, and downgraded 2019 shipment forecasts (Nikkei/Business Insider, June 2019). Qualcomm, Intel, Arm, and Google have all severed ties. While Huawei has 8-12 months of component stockpiles (CNBC, May 17), this is a ticking clock — if the ban persists, Huawei's phone and telecom equipment businesses face severe structural damage.

Second, the threat of $300B in additional tariffs on remaining Chinese exports (Trump threatened this on May 5, reiterated before G20) would push tariff coverage to nearly all Chinese exports to the US. However, as of the decision date, this remains a threat, not reality. Current tariff coverage is ~$250B at 25%, and China's Q1 2019 GDP held at 6.4% — beating expectations — with industrial production surging 8.5% in March (SCMP, April 17). The IMF's June 5 downgrade to 6.2% acknowledges trade risks but confirms stimulus is 'sufficient to stabilise growth.' Provincial growth targets have been slashed (SCMP, Jan 16), but the economy is not in freefall.

The action_score of -0.05 (negotiate, near neutral) reflects the following logic: (a) China should NOT escalate further before G20 — the economy is absorbing the current shock and Huawei has a stockpile buffer, but further US escalation (especially $300B tariffs or additional entity list additions like Hikvision) would push China toward genuine economic danger; (b) China should NOT concede — the unreliable entity list announcement (May 31) and rare earth signaling (Xi's Jiangxi visit May 20, NDRC threats May 28) have established credible retaliatory leverage that constrains US action; (c) the G20 meeting is imminent and both leaders have confirmed attendance after a June 18 phone call — this is the moment to negotiate, not to fire new salvos.

Second-order effects favor restraint: US companies (Qualcomm, Intel) are already lobbying Commerce to relax the Huawei ban (IT Pro, June 21), and IQE slashed revenue forecasts by £35M citing Huawei fallout. The US tech industry is an internal constraint on further escalation. Meanwhile, China's rare earth threat, while symbolically potent, is assessed by analysts as limited in practice (CNBC/Raymond James, June 3: 'impact on the US would be mild'; Reason, May 29: 'shooting blanks'). Deploying it now would burn a card for limited gain while confirming China as a risky supply source. Better to hold it in reserve.
key_factors: Huawei Entity List (May 16): 68 affiliates, Google/Qualcomm/Intel/Arm severed ties, 30% supply chain order cuts, 8-12 month stockpile buffer ticking
$300B tariff threat on remaining Chinese exports — not yet implemented but imminent if G20 fails
China's Q1 2019 GDP at 6.4% (beat expectations), industrial production +8.5% in March — economy absorbing shock but IMF downgraded to 6.2%
Unreliable entity list announced (May 31) — unplayed retaliatory leverage card, details not yet released
Rare earth signaling (Xi Jiangxi visit May 20, NDRC threats May 28) — symbolically potent but analysts assess practical impact as limited
G20 Osaka meeting confirmed for June 28-29, both leaders attending after June 18 phone call — critical negotiation window
US tech companies lobbying Commerce to relax Huawei ban — internal US constraint on further escalation

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
China announces it will establish an 'unreliable entity list' targeting foreign firms that cut supplies to Chinese companies for non-commercial reasons.
Trump and Xi agree by phone to meet at the G20 in Osaka.
Huawei has reportedly cut orders to suppliers by as much as 30% and has downgraded its smartphone shipments for 2019 following its placement on a US trade blacklist.
China's GDP expanded 6.4% in Q1 2019, beating expectations. Industrial production expanded 8.5% in March from a year earlier, the strongest growth since July 2014.
IMF cut China's 2019 GDP growth forecast to 6.2% citing trade tensions. 'The policy stimulus announced so far is sufficient to stabilise growth in 2019/20 despite the recent U.S. tariff hike.'
Raymond James: 'We are of the view that the impact on the U.S. would be mild, which is one reason why we are skeptical that Beijing would pull the trigger on this particular threat.'
